newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK-- Mkt still has more room to run.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK-- Mkt still has more room to run.

text.p: Now that the U.S. Treasury market has rallied to levels not seen in nearly four months, the questions going forward are: can prices continue to rise and yields drop further?
"We think there is more room left" to rally, said Larry Dyer, Treasury market strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp.
Dyer and others, though, believe the shorter end has largely hit its peak, while the longer end can still rally more.
"The bond is the cheap part of the curve," Dyer said. "Unless the market starts to price in an ease, the front end is pretty locked in place."

Late Friday, the 30-year bond was at 98-22/32, up 20/32, with its yield falling to 6.73 percent. The two-year note was up 3/32 at 100-13/32 to yield 6.03 percent. Earlier in the session, the two-year note's yield fell to 5.99 percent, falling below 6 percent for the first time since February 25.
"We have priced in no Fed for a long, long, long time," said Neil DeSarno, head trader at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp.
"The psychology has changed from a 50-50 possibility of a rate hike in July or the summer to almost nil," DeSarno said.
If the current bullish sentiment holds, players said the bond could fall to a yield of 6.5 percent and the two-year to 5.80-5.85 percent.

The problem facing the market is that with economic data in the upcoming week to be market friendly, there would be a tendency for dealers to continue to drive up prices. But, traders warned, there is little room to move at the shorter end and any attempt at a correction would mean overcoming a strong technical environment.

Data next week include May reports on consumer prices, housing starts and industrial production on Tuesday, revised first-quarter unit labor costs and the Fed's Beige Book on Wednesday, and April trade and the Phiadelphia Fed's June business outlook survey on Thursday.
But even if the data come in on the weak side, the upside is limited at the short end, players said.
As such, the yield curve is seen flattening, as the long end leads the rally.
Meanahile, the firm dollar and probability of further Fed coupon passes should help underpin the market.
"With no supply, the market can hold these levels," DeSarno said. "I think the market is overvalued but still in good technical shape. It will probably run into trouble when faced with supply."
The next round of Treasury auctions are June 24-25 when the Treasury sells two- and five-year notes.
In the meantime, Fed debates will continue to take center stage.
Dyer said a Fed rate hike can't be ruled out yet.
"Why would the Fed, who has highlighted concern over the low unemployment rate, move to the ease side?" he said. "Most signals are biased to tighten. That's the dominant view."
However, he added: "Everyone agrees the Fed does not have a lot to do. The economy, while hot, is not overheating and doesn't require a lot of tightening."
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867 ))
